claims.text: High-entropy alloys intrinsically exhibit sluggish diffusion kinetics.
Sluggish diffusion governs the surface segregation of reactive elements such as Cr and Al.
Controlled segregation of Cr and Al promotes formation of a dense oxide scale.
Controlled segregation of Cr and Al promotes an adherent oxide scale.
The dense, adherent oxide scale retards further oxidation.
The proposed initial alloy has a uniform, equiatomic distribution of reactive and non-reactive elements.
The relevant oxide scale is nanostructured and enriched in Cr and Al.
The relevant oxide scale has low defect density.
The relevant oxide scale adheres strongly to the substrate.
Sluggish matrix diffusion limits rapid bulk cation transport.
Sluggish matrix diffusion permits gradual, controlled migration of reactive elements to the surface.
Gradual migration of reactive elements facilitates formation of a continuous protective oxide layer.
A continuous protective oxide layer limits oxygen ingress and oxidation of the substrate.
Relative to binary or ternary alloys with similar reactive-element content, the high-entropy alloy will exhibit slower oxidation kinetics.
Slower oxidation will appear as lower and more consistent weight gain over time.
The high-entropy alloy will develop a denser and more adherent oxide scale than the conventional-alloy baseline.
The mechanism requires sufficient concentrations of reactive elements such as Cr and Al.
Compositional changes that alter diffusion kinetics may place an alloy outside the mechanism's applicability.
Extreme oxygen pressures or temperatures may place the oxidation behavior outside the mechanism's applicability.
The quantitative contribution of sluggish diffusion relative to scale-growth stresses and elemental interactions is not determined.
